name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_DIAG_Q01 - Structure and DNA length of a nucleosome

questiontext.text: The schematic diagram below represents a nucleosome in eukaryotic chromatin. Identify the parts labelled P and Q, and state the approximate length of DNA helix wrapped in a typical nucleosome.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a central spherical core labelled as the histone octamer, a ribbon-like strand labelled P wrapped around the core in nearly two turns, and an elongated protein labelled Q positioned at the entry and exit point of the wrapped strand.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
This represents the fundamental repeating unit of eukaryotic chromatin packaging, the nucleosome, where negatively charged DNA associates with positively charged basic histone proteins.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In eukaryotes, eight histone molecules form a histone octamer. Negatively charged DNA wraps around this positively charged octamer, and H1 histone acts as a linker protein sealing the DNA at the entry/exit site. A typical nucleosome contains \(200\text{ bp}\) of DNA helix.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The wrapped ribbon P corresponds to the DNA helix. The elongated clamp-like protein Q holding the DNA strands together at the side of the octamer corresponds to the H1 histone. The standard length of DNA helix associated with one nucleosome is \(200\text{ bp}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Comparing with the known structure of eukaryotic chromatin, P is the DNA helix, Q is the H1 histone, and the length of DNA in a typical nucleosome is \(200\text{ bp}\).

answer.text: P = DNA helix, Q = H1 histone, Length = \(200\text{ bp}\)
P = H1 histone, Q = DNA helix, Length = \(200\text{ bp}\)
P = DNA helix, Q = Non-histone chromosomal protein, Length = \(340\text{ bp}\)
P = RNA primer, Q = H1 histone, Length = \(100\text{ bp}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_DIAG_Q02 - Direction of synthesis at DNA replication fork

questiontext.text: The diagram below illustrates a DNA replication fork. Based on the polarity of the parental template strands, identify the direction of polymerisation of the newly synthesised strands X and Y, and the enzyme required to join the fragments in strand Y.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a Y-shaped replication fork formed by two antiparallel parental template strands. The left template strand runs \(3' \to 5'\) towards the fork, and the right template strand runs \(5' \to 3'\) towards the fork. Strand X is synthesised continuously towards the fork, while strand Y is synthesised as short discontinuous fragments away from the fork.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The newly synthesised strands must be antiparallel and complementary to their respective template strands.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
DNA-dependent DNA polymerases catalyse the polymerisation of deoxynucleotides only in one direction: \(5' \to 3'\). Discontinuously synthesised DNA fragments are later joined together by the enzyme DNA ligase.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
On the \(3' \to 5'\) template strand (left), the \(5' \to 3'\) direction of synthesis moves towards the opening fork, allowing continuous synthesis of strand X in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction. On the \(5' \to 3'\) template strand (right), the \(5' \to 3'\) direction of synthesis moves away from the fork, producing discontinuous fragments (strand Y), each still synthesised in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction. These fragments are joined by DNA ligase.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Both X and Y are synthesised in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction, and the fragments of strand Y are joined by DNA ligase.

answer.text: X is synthesised \(3' \to 5'\) continuously; Y is synthesised \(5' \to 3'\) discontinuously; joined by DNA polymerase
X is synthesised \(5' \to 3'\) discontinuously; Y is synthesised \(3' \to 5'\) continuously; joined by DNA ligase
Both X and Y are synthesised in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction; fragments of Y are joined by DNA ligase
Both X and Y are synthesised in the \(3' \to 5'\) direction; fragments of Y are joined by RNA polymerase

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_DIAG_Q03 - Switching promoter and terminator in transcription unit

questiontext.text: The schematic diagram represents a transcription unit in DNA. What would happen if the positions of Region P (Promoter) and Region Q (Terminator) are interchanged?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a transcription unit with a structural gene flanked by Region P (promoter) at the \(5'\)-end of the coding strand and Region Q (terminator) at the \(3'\)-end of the coding strand. The top \(3' \to 5'\) strand is labelled as the template strand, and the bottom \(5' \to 3'\) strand is labelled as the coding strand.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In a transcription unit, all positional references (upstream \(5'\) and downstream \(3'\)) are made with respect to the polarity of the coding strand.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyses polymerisation only in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction, which requires a template strand with \(3' \to 5'\) polarity relative to the direction of transcription from promoter to terminator. The presence of the promoter defines which strand acts as the template strand and which acts as the coding strand.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
If the positions of Region P (promoter) and Region Q (terminator) are switched, RNA polymerase will bind at the right end and transcribe towards the left end. To polymerise RNA in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction from right to left, the enzyme must use the bottom strand (which reads \(3' \to 5'\) from right to left) as the template strand, while the top strand becomes the coding strand.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Switching the positions of the promoter and terminator reverses the definitions of the template strand and the coding strand.

answer.text: Transcription terminates immediately without forming any RNA
The roles of the template strand and coding strand are reversed
RNA polymerase binds to Region Q and polymerises RNA in the \(3' \to 5'\) direction
Only introns are transcribed instead of exons

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_DIAG_Q04 - Interpreting VNTR banding pattern in DNA fingerprinting

questiontext.text: The diagram below shows an autoradiogram of VNTR bands separated by gel electrophoresis for DNA collected from a crime scene (C) and two suspects (A and B), along with a scale indicating the number of short tandem repeats. Which conclusion is supported by this banding pattern?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The autoradiogram displays VNTR bands across three lanes: crime scene DNA (C), suspect A, and suspect B, aligned against a vertical scale of short tandem repeat numbers from \(1\) to \(12\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Each band corresponds to an allele of a specific VNTR locus, where a higher number of tandem repeats migrates more slowly and appears higher up in the gel.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
VNTR copy numbers show high polymorphism among individuals, producing a unique characteristic banding pattern for every individual (except monozygotic twins). A forensic match requires the complete banding profile of the crime scene sample to align with that of the suspect.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Reading the repeat numbers from the scale: Lane C has bands at \(11, 9, 8, 6, 5,\) and \(2\) repeats. Lane A has bands at \(10, 8, 7, 5, 4,\) and \(3\) repeats, matching only two bands (\(8\) and \(5\)) by chance. Lane B has bands at \(11, 9, 8, 6, 5,\) and \(2\) repeats, matching every single band of Lane C in both position and repeat number.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because all six VNTR bands in the crime scene DNA match those of Individual B identically, the crime scene DNA belongs to Individual B.

answer.text: The crime scene DNA matches Individual A because both share a band at \(8\) tandem repeats
Neither Individual A nor Individual B matches the crime scene DNA because VNTRs vary between tissues
Individual A and Individual B are monozygotic twins because they share a band at \(5\) tandem repeats
The crime scene DNA matches Individual B because all VNTR band sizes (\(11, 9, 8, 6, 5,\) and \(2\) repeats) are identical
